**Short answer:** The vault can't answer this directly. None of its 12 sources has Paul Graham saying whether a founder outside the US needs to move to Silicon Valley. What it does have points one way: PG treats Silicon Valley as special, and YC moved its own program there on purpose. But he also chose to live in England himself.

**What they've said**
- **PG, *Superlinear Returns* (2023)**, on why the Valley is a good place to fail: "This is one reason Silicon Valley is so tolerant of failure. People in Silicon Valley aren't blindly tolerant of failure. They'll only continue to bet on you if you're learning from your failures." ([web-76d87c7c2e80](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html); by: pg). His point is that the Valley's investors will keep backing a founder who is getting better, even after a failure. Other places are less likely to.
- **Livingston (2018)**, on why YC left Boston: "we also decided that we'd fund the next batch in Silicon Valley we knew that a lot of people would copy us and we didn't want someone else to be the Y Combinator of Silicon Valley we wanted to be that ourselves" ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 12:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=722s); by: livingston)
- **Livingston (2024)**: "we were in Boston which was even more different than Silicon Valley" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 2:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=136s); by: livingston). In context, Boston only had VCs writing million-dollar checks and very few angels.

**What they've done:** YC started in Cambridge, Massachusetts and moved to Silicon Valley within months ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 25:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1510s)). PG himself now lives in England. Livingston says it gives him little startup stimulation: "we don't get a lot of that stimulation in England he comes back and all of a sudden it's this like fire hose of startups and new ideas" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 10:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=608s); by: livingston). That's her description of him, not his own words.

**Where this is uncertain:**
- The vault is missing the PG essays that actually deal with this question: *How to Be Silicon Valley* (2006), *Why Startups Condense in America* (2006), *Cities and Ambition* (2008) and *Can You Buy a Silicon Valley? Maybe.* (2009). They are on paulgraham.com but were never added to this vault, so nothing here quotes them. I'd add and compile them before relying on any answer to this question.
- PG co-founded YC and runs it from the Valley, so he isn't neutral on whether founders should come there (the vault's profile flags this).
- He lives in England and is still a successful investor and writer. That suggests he doesn't see the Valley as necessary for everyone at every stage. But he's no longer running a startup, so it tells you little about what a founder should do.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the sources above, not his words):
- PG would probably not tell you to move permanently right away. He would tell you to spend real time in Silicon Valley, especially when you raise money. The reasons he gives are about the place itself: investors who will back you even after you fail, early-stage money that Boston lacked in 2005, and the "fire hose" of ideas he still goes back for.
- From Stockholm, the practical version is: build and get your first users at home, then go to the Valley for fundraising or a program like YC. If your investors, customers or best hires end up there, move.
- The case for staying is weakest if your plan relies on raising US-style seed and Series A rounds, and strongest if your customers and team are in Europe.
- Outside this vault, from general knowledge and not verified here: in *Cities and Ambition* PG argues that each city sends its own message about what matters, and that Silicon Valley's is about being more powerful. In the startup essays above he argues that startup hubs are hard to recreate elsewhere. Both would push his answer further toward "spend serious time there."

Should I add those four essays to the vault and compile them? Then this could become a cited answer instead of an extrapolation.

**Short answer:** The vault has nothing from Paul Graham on brand versus product as such. Going by what he has said, he would call winning on brand instead of product a version of the trick he warns founders against. In a startup "there's only users," and you "only prosper to the extent that" you've made something they want. He sees brand as something that builds up on top of a good product, not as a substitute for one.

**What they've said**

- **Users only care whether the product works.** PG says starting a startup "is where gaming the system stops working." "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want, right?" Then: "So, you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extent that you do." ([2014 Stanford lecture "Before the Startup" @ 11:00–12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=660s))
- **Tricks matter far less than the real problem.** "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." (same lecture @ 13:17) He would likely put brand-first strategy with growth hacks: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." (@ 10:26)
- **His version of marketing is short.** "The way to make your startup grow is to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it." (@ 10:26) The telling comes second, and the love has to be real.
- **Founders who play house.** He calls it a characteristic mistake to imitate "all the outward forms of starting a startup" while neglecting "the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want." (@ 7:32) A polished brand around a weak product is that kind of outward form.
- **Faking can fool investors, but it costs you.** "Faking does work to some extent with investors." But "You're playing a confidence trick on yourself. You're wasting your own time, because the startup is doomed." (@ 12:43)
- **Brand does compound, once you have one.** In *Superlinear Returns* (2023) he lists "growing an audience or brand" as work that compounds, "in the sense that doing well in one cycle causes you to do better in the next." ([paulgraham.com/superlinear.html](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)) So he isn't against brand. He treats it as something that builds on earlier success.
- **Mediocre products that win on habit or brand are targets.** "If a company makes a product that people dislike yet still buy, then presumably they'd buy a better alternative if you made one." (same essay) In his view, a company winning on brand without the product is the one a startup should go after.

**What other YC partners said:** In a 2022 YC talk, Seibel and Caldwell describe Stripe's "really clever brand promise or marketing stance": "to try to make the most beautiful website they could with the most beautiful documentation," aimed at developers. ([Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From? @ 14:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=886s)) The transcript doesn't make clear which of the two says it. Either way, the brand there was the product: the docs were what customers were using. The same talk's main point is that Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe won with products 10x better than bad incumbents.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The vault has no source where PG talks about consumer brands, luxury goods or other commodity categories, where brand plausibly *is* the product.
- The 2014 lecture was aimed at Stanford students building software, so "users only care whether your software does what they want" is framed for that audience.

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources, built from the principles above)
- PG would probably say that for an early startup, "brand" usually means users love the product and talk about it. That kind of brand follows from the product, and you can't get it first and fill in the product later.
- He'd probably accept brand as a real moat later on, as something that compounds (*Superlinear Returns*). He'd still see a company leaning on brand to hold up a mediocre product as exposed to a startup with a better one. That's his "mediocre yet still popular" test.
- If your product category really can't be told apart from the competition, he'd likely ask why you're in it. He tells founders to look for problems where they can be much better, not markets where marketing is the only lever.

One caveat of my own: in consumer goods (beverages, fashion, cosmetics), brand-led startups do win. The vault doesn't show PG ever taking that case on, so this answer fits tech startups much better than consumer brands.

**Short answer:** No source in the vault covers this. `yc-pre` lists Sam Altman as a member, but it contains nothing he said or wrote. There are no Altman statements on AI or on anything else, so I can't give a grounded answer.

**What the vault has on Altman:** he is only mentioned by other people.
- Livingston (2018) says "Sam Altman's geolocation startup" was in YC's first batch (yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 11:28, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=688s).
- Livingston (2024): "Sam Altman was impressive at age 19." She also says that when PG suggested he wait a year, he replied "I'm a sophomore and I'm coming" (yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 54:34, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=3274s).
- In PG's 2014 Stanford lecture, "Sam" is the course host PG speaks to. Altman doesn't speak in the transcript.

**Extrapolation:** I can't do a sound one here. Extrapolating means reasoning from principles he has stated, and the vault has none from him. Using PG's AI concern instead (his 2024 essay *Writes and Write-Nots* predicts AI will leave few people able to write) would put PG's view in Altman's mouth, so I won't.

**Outside the vault** (from my general knowledge, not checked against any source here): Altman has said publicly that the worst case is catastrophic. In a 2023 interview he called it "lights out for all of us." He has also talked about misuse of powerful models, and about society not adapting fast enough even if nothing dramatic happens. Treat this as uncited background, not a vault answer.

**Gap:** the vault is configured for Altman but no sources by him have been added. To answer this properly, add his blog (blog.samaltman.com, including "The Gentle Singularity" and "Three Observations") and a few of his long interviews. Then run discover, fetch and compile. Want me to set that up?

**Short answer:** The vault has no talk where Seibel covers fundraising directly. What it does have points one way: months spent on a deck and investor meetings is time not spent building something customers use. He'd also say a "no" from investors tells you very little about your company. Build, launch and get users, then raise on traction.

**What he has said**
- **Pitch deck work is lower value than building.** "So spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([How to Plan an MVP, 2019 @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s)). He says this right after arguing that you can't know if a product works until it's in front of people.
- **Investor opinions shouldn't steer the product.** He mocks founders who change what they're building after an investor says "Oh, that could never be a company." His aside: "Because investors know everything." ([same talk @ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s)). It's sarcasm, not respect for investor judgment.
- **Investor rejection isn't a verdict.** About Coinbase struggling to raise at Demo Day: "If he had taken the demo day signal, the investor signal of 'oh, we don't want to give you money', and quit, we don't have Coinbase." ([Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?, 2022 @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s)). Also: "If they had listened to most of the investors or most of the founders at the time, Airbnb wouldn't exist." (@ 7:08)
- **Ignore experts who aren't users.** "Especially you shouldn't care if they're not going to be users, if they have no experience with the pain of using the existing product." (@ [19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1182s)). Most seed investors fit that description.
- **Launch to customers, not to an audience.** "Let's push the press launch off and let's push the get any customers launch really really soon." ([2019 @ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s))

**Same view from YC (Paul Graham, not Seibel):** "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money. Than someone who knows every trick in the book, but has a flat usage graph." ([Before the Startup, 2014 @ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))

**Where this is uncertain**
- The vault has two Seibel sources, the 2019 MVP talk and a 2022 talk on startup ideas. It doesn't include his material on how to run a raise: round size, timelines, follow-up meetings or how to handle investors. Anything specific about your process is beyond what the vault supports.
- His examples (Airbnb, Coinbase, Twitch) are huge survivors. Investors were wrong about those, but that doesn't show they're usually wrong.

**Extrapolation (not from the sources)**
Based on the principles above, here's what Seibel would likely say:
1. **Ask what months of rejection are telling you.** If investors aren't biting, the most likely reason is that you lack traction, not that your deck is weak. Another round of deck polish probably won't fix that.
2. **Stop treating follow-up meetings as progress.** Like a press launch, a meeting can feel like work without being the real thing. The real thing is customers using the product.
3. **Put most of your time back into the product.** Time-box an MVP to weeks, ship it, get any customers, talk to them and iterate. Keep fundraising light or pause it until there's a usage or revenue graph to show.
4. **Don't change your idea because investors said no.** Write your spec down so investor feedback can't quietly move it. Change course because of what users tell you.
5. **When you raise again, make traction the pitch.** The pitch should be a short story built around real numbers.

My own caveat: if your runway is about to run out, "stop raising and build" may not be possible. That constraint isn't something these sources address.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault has Dalton Caldwell answering "pick a safe idea to improve my odds." His one talk in the vault (2022, with Michael Seibel) argues that you can't tell which ideas are safe. The ideas that became YC's biggest wins looked bad, hard or small at the start, including to him.

**What he's said**

Source: *Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?*, Seibel & Caldwell, 2022: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8

- **His own judgment of Airbnb was wrong.** Airbnb "kind of felt like the third-rate entrant to a crowded space at the time" (@ 1:38, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=98s). Renting a room with the host there was "like the ultimate unappealing, scary, bad thing that no one wanted to do" (@ 4:57).
- **The idea that looked modest was big.** Even Brian Armstrong "under accounted the simple promise of buying bitcoin in a non-sketchy way with a debit card in the US and not getting hacked and losing all your money. That was enough." (@ 10:56; medium confidence that Caldwell is the speaker). Armstrong had applied to YC with peer-to-peer transfers. The plain version turned into a company worth about $100B.
- **The winning idea was hard to build.** Before Stripe, getting a merchant account "was like applying for a mortgage" (@ 12:34). He calls payments "a possible thing to do, but I would call it gnarly and the opposite of easy in every way" (@ 13:08).
- **Outsiders didn't see YC companies as risky.** They saw them as "the third-rate knock-off version of something actually good" (@ 18:03; medium confidence on the speaker).

**What he's done:** He passed on buying Bitcoin in 2011 because the process "seemed too much like a total scam" (@ 7:42), so he played it safe and missed out. He joined the Stripe beta as one of its first 100 customers because "I hadn't even seen it yet, I just knew I wanted it." (@ 13:40)

**Seibel in the same talk (his words, not Caldwell's):** Don't care if experts think it's a bad idea, "especially… if they're not going to be users." Also: "Be very careful about your initial market math" and "Don't be discouraged if someone's like, that's a tiny market." (@ 19:42–20:16)

**Where this is uncertain**
- The talk looks back at three of YC's biggest wins: Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe. It says nothing about how many ambitious ideas failed, so it can't show that ambition improves your odds.
- The transcript doesn't label speakers, so some lines are only attributed to Caldwell with medium confidence.
- Caldwell never compares a safe, modest company with an ambitious one. He also never covers the case where a modest outcome is the goal, such as a small profitable business.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the points above; he didn't say this)

Caldwell would probably push back on the idea that a "safe" idea exists:

1. **You can't judge safety ahead of time.** He judged Airbnb and Bitcoin wrong, and so did most investors. If someone this experienced can't tell good ideas from bad ones early, an idea that feels safe to you may just be one that sounds acceptable to other people.
2. **The real safety test is something else.** His talk keeps coming back to three things: you have the problem yourself, the existing products are bad, and a 10x better version is possible. He'd likely say those reduce your risk more than a modest-sounding pitch does.
3. **Keep the first version small, not the goal.** Coinbase started as "buy Bitcoin without getting robbed." A narrow, simple starting point fits his view. Choosing an idea because its ceiling is low does not.
4. **Being hard is not a reason to avoid an idea.** He called Stripe "gnarly and the opposite of easy," and it worked because the problem was painful enough.

So his likely answer: don't choose based on whether the idea seems safe. Choose a problem you have, where the current options are bad, and start with the simplest version.

My own view, separately: survivorship bias weakens this advice. If you need a reliable income, a modest idea can be a reasonable choice. YC's advice assumes you're aiming for a huge outcome.

**Short answer:** The vault has nothing from Garry Tan on who owns AI workflows or skill files. What it has from him is a few remarks about YC fund returns, made in one 2024 podcast. The closest material is Paul Graham's view that your work should be "something you carry with you from job to job." That points to yes, it matters, and you should keep what compounds. But that's PG, not Tan.

**What Tan has said (all of it in this vault)**
- Tan is a member of the vault, but he only appears in one source: the 2024 Lightcone episode with Jessica Livingston ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY)). Everything attributed to him there is about funds. He says funding a whole YC batch would beat "most of the VC funds returns", and he mentions his own fund, Initialized (@ 40:30).
- He says nothing in the vault about AI, agents, employment or who owns work. The only mentions of "AI" in that episode are passing comments by other speakers.

**Closest related view (Paul Graham, not Tan)**
From *Superlinear Returns* (2023, [paulgraham.com/superlinear.html](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)):
- "Are there general rules for finding situations with superlinear returns? The most obvious one is to seek work that compounds."
- Work compounds "when you're building infrastructure, or growing an audience or brand. Or work can compound by teaching you, since learning compounds."
- "Not to equate work with a job." … "For someone like that, their work is something they carry with them from job to job, if they have jobs at all."
- When he was young, artists appealed to him partly because they "seemed least at the mercy of organizations."

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault is named `yc-pre` and its newest source is from 2025. Tan's public comments on AI agents and tooling aren't in it. Any statements of his on this topic would come from sources nobody has added yet.

**Extrapolation (from PG's principles, not Tan's statements)**
- **The skill matters more than the files.** On PG's "learning compounds" principle, the most valuable thing you're building is your ability to design agent workflows. You keep that no matter who owns the files.
- **The files are infrastructure, and infrastructure compounds.** If your employer owns them, the compounding stays with them when you leave. On PG's view, that's a reason to notice which parts are general (your methods, patterns and personal tooling) and which are tied to your employer. Your contract and IP terms decide what you can actually take. Read them before copying anything out.
- **This is the kind of thing YC founders come from.** PG's "be your own user" and "problems you and your peers have" ideas suggest that if you keep building the same scaffolding at work, the people around you probably need it too. That's an idea worth thinking about on your own time, with your own resources.

I can't honestly extrapolate this to Tan himself: the vault doesn't document any of his principles beyond fund returns. To get a Tan-specific answer, I can add his recent talks or X/blog posts on AI agents to the vault, compile them, and answer again.

**Short answer:** No. Michael Seibel would tell you to stop adding features and launch now. He'd call your 3-month, feature-heavy pre-launch the exact failure his MVP talk warns about. The vault has nothing from Dalton Caldwell on launch timing, so his part below is extrapolation.

**What Seibel has said** (2019 Startup School, "How to Plan an MVP": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM)
- **Launch something bad, quickly.** "If you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." ([@ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)) He counts "launched" as soon as you have any customers: "How about launch is when you get any customers." (@ 10:07)
- **Weeks, not months.** "You should be able to build it fast in weeks, not months." (@ 4:29) You're 3 months in, so by his standard you're already late.
- **Your situation, almost word for word:** "It's really easy to change what you're working on before you ever launch it because you never write it down… And so, your three-week plan turns into a three-month plan." (@ 11:44) Saying yes to every request on every call is how the spec keeps moving.
- **Cut, don't add.** "Just cut the stuff that clearly isn't important. Um, and if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things." (@ 12:17)
- **Serve a few users' biggest problems, ignore the rest.** "They should just focus on a small set of initial users and their highest order problems and then ignore the rest until later." (@ 5:03)
- **Feature requests can't tell you what people want.** "It might turn out the full thing that you want to build isn't what your customers want at all." (@ 3:19) He also says "it's a lot harder to learn from your customers when they don't have a product they can play with. … If you put the thing in front of them and it doesn't solve their problem, you know right away." (@ 10:39) Requests made on a call are guesses. Usage is real evidence.
- **Don't get attached to what you've built.** "A lot of founders once they've figured out how to build something fall in love with it." (@ 3:19) He says to hold the problem and the customer tightly and the solution loosely.
- **Delay keeps going until you launch.** "If you don't have anything out in the world, it's very easy to just delay, delay, delay, delay." (@ 12:51) He also says "you'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." (@ 2:14)

**What Seibel has done:** his examples are first versions most people would call "pretty shitty" (@ 7:52). Airbnb launched with no payments and no map view. Justin.tv had one channel. At Stripe, the founders went to customers' offices and integrated it by hand. Justin.tv was his own company.

**Caldwell:** The vault has one talk with him (2022, with Seibel: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8), and it's about where ideas come from, not about launch timing. The relevant point from it is Seibel's, not his: Airbnb found its most important missing feature, payments, only by using the live product ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=264s)). You find those features after launch, not on discovery calls.

**Where this is uncertain:**
- Seibel's advice dates from 2019, before Claude Code. The vault has nothing from either of them on AI making features cheap to build.
- His examples are billion-dollar companies, so survivorship bias applies.
- He allows a "heavy MVP" only for regulated fields or hard tech (insurance, banking, rockets, biotech). If you're in one of those, the advice changes somewhat.

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources, reasoned from the principles above)
- **On Claude Code:** Seibel's argument never depended on building being slow. It depends on learning only happening after launch, and on the spec growing when nothing is in front of users. Cheap features make the problem worse because nothing slows the spec down. He would probably say that being able to build something doesn't mean you should.
- **What he'd likely tell you to do this week:**
  1. Write down the 1–2 highest-order problems of a small group of users you can name.
  2. Put everything else behind a flag or remove it.
  3. Get the product to those users within days.
  4. Stop collecting requests on calls and watch what people actually use.
- **Caldwell, judging from how he talks about Stripe:** he'd likely push you to obsess over one core thing that your target user would "just freak out about" (@ 15:18), rather than add breadth.

My own view: I agree with all of this. One thing to watch is that a large unused feature set costs you a lot in maintenance and support as a solo founder, even when the code was cheap to write.

I couldn't find anything in the vault where Michael Seibel talks about cofounder breakups, vesting disputes or lawyers. So the answer below is mostly my extrapolation from things he says elsewhere, and I've labelled it.

**Short answer:** No source in the vault covers this. Based on what he does say, Seibel would probably tell you that fighting over equity in a company with no users or traction is a fight over close to nothing, paid for with your most limited resources: time and cash. Settle quickly on the terms your vesting agreement already sets, then go back to building or start the next thing.

**What the vault actually has**
- **Seibel:** his two sources in the vault are a 2019 lecture on planning an MVP and a 2022 talk with Dalton Caldwell on startup ideas. Neither mentions cofounders splitting up, equity or legal disputes. The profile says he's credible on "building and launching first products" and doesn't list cofounder conflict.
- **PG (2014)** describes your situation, though he gives no advice on what to do once you're in it: "There's a lot of people who are really good at seeming likeable for a while. Just wait till your interests are opposed and then you'll see." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=313s) @ 5:13)
- **Jessica Livingston (2018)** treats the cofounder relationship as the main thing YC judged: "most importantly, what was the relationship between the co-founders like?" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s) @ 14:51). Her rule for picking one is "Find a co-founder with complimentary skills but the same moral compass as you." (@ 23:59)

**Extrapolation (not in the sources)**, built from Seibel's documented principles:
1. **He measures progress by contact with customers.** He says: "You'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=134s) @ 2:14). Each month the lawyers trade letters is a month nobody spends shipping or talking to users. He'd probably see that as the real cost, bigger than whatever stake is being argued over.
2. **Without product-market fit, the equity is worth little.** Nine months in with no traction, the shares are worth roughly zero until someone builds something people want. Legal fees are real money now. He'd likely tell you to work out the cash you'll spend on lawyers against the realistic value of the disputed shares.
3. **"Hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely."** ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s) @ 3:19). If you're the one continuing, your commitment is to the problem and the customer, not to this particular company or cap table. If his stake would scare off investors, restarting clean on the same problem could cost less than winning the fight.
4. **Practical reading (mine, not legal advice):** vested shares normally belong to him. The usual fight is over unvested shares and the company's repurchase right. If your documents set this out, the quickest outcome is to apply them as written and sign mutual releases. If the documents don't, that was the mistake, and the question is how cheaply you can get out of it.

**Where this is uncertain:** Seibel has spoken publicly about cofounder disputes outside these sources, but none of that is in the vault, so I haven't put words in his mouth. If you want an answer grounded in what he actually said, I can find and add those talks or posts to `yc-pre` and run the question again.

**Short answer:** The vault doesn't have anything from Garry Tan on AI agents. Nobody in it talks about agents at all. Everything below about "this week" is my extrapolation from YC's documented principles, mostly Paul Graham's and Michael Seibel's, not Tan's own words.

**What the vault has from Garry Tan**

There are only three statements from him, all from one 2024 podcast with Jessica Livingston ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY)). They cover YC's fund returns and his own fund, Initialized, plus his time as YC's designer in residence. None of them is about AI, tools or how founders should work. The vault's own profile describes him as a YC promoter whose claims about returns come without figures.

The only AI material in the vault is Paul Graham's 2024 essay *Writes and Write-Nots* ([essay](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html)). It's a warning, not a how-to: "AI has blown this world open. Almost all pressure to write has dissipated." He adds that writing is thinking, so a world split into people who write and people who don't "will be a world of thinks and think-nots."

**Extrapolation** (from YC principles in the vault, not from Tan)

1. **Use agents on your own work, not as a research project.** Seibel says "It's even more helpful if you're your own user so you can tell whether your product's working for you" ([video @ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=33s)). Pick one painful task you repeat every week, like support triage, a slow coding chore, sales follow-ups or research, and give it to an agent. Don't start by surveying frameworks.
2. **Give it a time limit and cut the plan down.** Seibel says to time-box the spec and then "cut the stuff that clearly isn't important. Um, and if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things" ([@ 12:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=737s)). One working agent workflow by Friday beats a plan to change the whole company.
3. **Get it working on real work quickly, even if it's rough.** "Launch something bad quickly" ([@ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)). The internal version: run the agent on real tasks this week and see where it breaks. "If you put the thing in front of them and it doesn't solve their problem, you know right away" ([@ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s)).
4. **Learn by doing, not by reading.** PG: "What do you do in the face of uncertainty? Get more certainty. And probably the best way to do that is to try working on things you're interested in" ([essay](https://paulgraham.com/when.html)). Not knowing where to begin is the kind of ignorance that only hands-on use fixes.
5. **Treat it as getting to the edge of the technology.** PG: "Get yourself to the leading edge of some technology, to, as Paul Buchheit put it, live in the future" ([video @ 29:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1746s)). The founders who use agents daily will notice "something that ought to exist" that others miss. That could also be your next product idea.
6. **Keep the thinking yourself.** Following PG's essay, let agents do the execution, but write your own strategy, investor updates and product reasoning.

## What he's said (grounded, PG only)

**1. "Make something people want," and don't play house.** He calls the most common mistake going through the motions of a startup "while imitating all the outward forms of starting a startup, they have neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want" ([2014 lecture @ 7:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=452s)). "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users" (@ 12:10). Faking "does work to some extent with investors," but then "you're playing a confidence trick on yourself" ([@ 12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=763s)).

**2. Expertise in your users, not in the category.** "What you need to know to succeed in a startup is not expertise in startups, what you need is expertise in your own users" ([@ 5:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=347s)). And "You can't learn those, until you actually start the company" ([@ 17:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1069s)).

**3. Did the idea come from living in the future?** He says to "get yourself to the leading edge of some technology... live in the future," where "you'll know they're something that ought to exist" ([@ 29:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1746s)). His example is a grad student who wrote voice-over-IP software to call his girlfriend in Taiwan "without paying for long distance calls," because "he was an expert on networks" ([@ 29:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1779s)). He also warns that ideas you make a conscious effort to think up come out "bad and plausible sounding" ([@ 24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s)).

**4. If something is bad but everyone still uses it, find out why.** "If a company makes a product that people dislike yet still buy, then presumably they'd buy a better alternative." But "when something is popular despite being mediocre, there's often a hidden reason why. Perhaps monopoly or regulation make it hard to compete" ([*Superlinear Returns*, 2023](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)).

**5. Growth rate and things that don't scale.** YC has founders "focus on growth rate rather than absolute numbers," and "if you pay a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers, ideally you'll kick off exponential growth by word of mouth" ([*Superlinear Returns*](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). Also: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit" ([@ 10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s)).

## Extrapolation (my reasoning from the principles above, not his words)
These are the questions I'd expect him to press on, each tied to a principle above:

1. **"Who used it this week, and what did they buy?"** (principles 1 and 5) Agent payments is a hyped category, which makes it easy to play house: a protocol, partnerships, a waitlist. He'd want the names of a few agent builders whose agents actually complete purchases through you, and your week-over-week growth in real transactions. Signups wouldn't count.
2. **"Are you the voice-over-IP guy?"** (principle 3) Did you run into this while building agents that kept failing at checkout? Or did you decide that agents will need wallets and work backwards from there? The second route is how you get his "bad and plausible sounding" ideas.
3. **"Who exactly is the user: the agent developer, the merchant, or the person whose money it is?"** (principle 2) Stripe won by obsessing over one customer, the developer. He'd push you to pick one side and know it better than anyone.
4. **"What's the hidden reason this isn't solved?"** (principle 4) Agents can already fill in card forms. Whatever stops them is probably not the payment rail itself. More likely it's merchants blocking bots, fraud and chargeback liability, or who is accountable when an agent buys the wrong thing. If you can't name the real blocker, he'd suspect you're fixing the wrong layer.
5. **"Do it by hand first."** (principle 5, plus the Stripe story) Take one agent product and a handful of merchants, wire them up yourselves, and get money moving before you design a general standard.

My own view, separate from his: point 4 is probably the one that decides whether this is a company, because the hard part of agent commerce tends to be on the merchant and liability side, not the payment API.
